content: Leg cramps are a frequent issue during pregnancy, and various treatments have been explored to address them, including medications, electrolyte and vitamin supplementation, and non-pharmacological approaches. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of these interventions. The evidence was derived from eight small randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 576 pregnant women. However, the studies had significant limitations, including small sample sizes, inconsistent reporting of outcomes, and low or very low certainty of evidence. Oral Magnesium vs. Placebo/No Treatment The effect of oral magnesium on the frequency of leg cramps was inconsistent. In one study, women receiving magnesium were more likely to report no leg cramps after treatment (risk ratio [RR] 5.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.35 to 23.68, low-certainty evidence). Additionally, fewer women reported experiencing leg cramps twice weekly (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.80), and more women reported a 50% reduction in the number of leg cramps (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.86). However, other findings suggested that magnesium might have little to no effect on cramp frequency during different treatment periods. Regarding pain intensity, the results were similarly inconsistent. One study found that magnesium might have little or no effect on the mean total pain score (mean difference [MD] 1.80, 95% CI -3.10 to 6.70, low-certainty evidence). Another study provided very uncertain evidence about magnesium's effect on pain intensity, while a third study suggested that magnesium might reduce pain intensity as measured by a visual analogue scale (MD -17.50, 95% CI -34.68 to -0.32, low-certainty evidence). For other outcomes, such as cramp duration, composite symptoms, and side effects (e.g., nausea and diarrhea), magnesium appeared to have little or no effect, with evidence rated as low to very low certainty. Oral Calcium vs. Placebo/No Treatment The evidence regarding the effect of calcium supplementation on leg cramp frequency was unclear due to very low certainty. One study suggested that calcium might reduce the frequency of leg cramps, with more women reporting no cramps after treatment (RR 8.59, 95% CI 1.19 to 62.07, very low-certainty evidence). Another small study indicated that the mean frequency of leg cramps might be slightly lower with calcium supplementation (MD -0.53, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.34, low-certainty evidence). Oral Vitamin B vs. No Treatment A single small trial suggested that oral vitamin B supplementation might reduce the frequency and intensity of leg cramps as a combined outcome (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.73, low-certainty evidence). However, the study did not report on the frequency of leg cramps as an individual outcome, and no data on side effects were available. Oral Calcium vs. Oral Vitamin C The evidence comparing calcium and vitamin C for leg cramp frequency was very uncertain. One study found no clear difference between the two interventions (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.53 to 3.38, very low-certainty evidence). Oral Vitamin D vs. Placebo One trial involving 84 women found that vitamin D supplementation might make little or no difference in the frequency of leg cramps compared to placebo at three weeks (MD 2.06, 95% CI 0.58 to 3.54) or six weeks after treatment (MD 1.53, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.94). Oral Calcium-Vitamin D vs. Placebo In the same trial, oral calcium-vitamin D supplementation appeared to have little or no effect on the frequency of leg cramps compared to placebo at three weeks (MD -0.30, 95% CI -1.55 to 0.95) or six weeks (MD 0.03, 95% CI -1.30 to 1.36). Oral Calcium-Vitamin D vs. Vitamin D The same trial also compared oral calcium-vitamin D supplementation to vitamin D alone. The results suggested little or no difference in leg cramp frequency at three weeks (MD -1.35, 95% CI -2.84 to 0.14) or six weeks (MD -1.10, 95% CI -2.69 to 0.49). Authors' Conclusions The evidence reviewed does not provide clear support for the effectiveness of any specific intervention for treating leg cramps during pregnancy. The primary limitations were the small size of the trials, inconsistent reporting of outcomes, and low or very low certainty of evidence. Adverse outcomes were not adequately reported, except for side effects associated with magnesium supplementation. The lack of consistency in outcome measurement and reporting precluded meta-analyses. Future research should focus on developing a standardized set of outcomes to measure the frequency, intensity, and duration of leg cramps, enabling more robust and comparable investigations.
